source.title: In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in large language models
source.authors: Hua-Dong Xiong; Ji-An Li; Jiaqi Huang; Robert C. Wilson; Kwonjoon Lee; Xue-Xin Wei

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses superposition as a framework for in-context working-memory interference, but does not test whether individual neurons in trained networks are polysemantic or whether polysemanticity is caused by feature-capacity pressure.
record.gate_note: The study measures working-memory performance and entanglement among contextual memory representations, not neuron responses to unrelated inputs. These are related findings, recorded under fits_no_version; no claim version is tested. The embedded N-back task instructions address the evaluated models, not an AI reading or reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the superposition framing to explain in-context working-memory interference in LLMs. It measures N-back behaviour, attention profiles, residual-stream geometry and letter-identity suppression. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common such neurons are, or what causes them, so no version of the polysemantic-neuron claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct, with one addition. The authors frame the overlap as 'in-context superposition', an online analogue of feature superposition. They state the evidence is geometric and does not establish a dimensional bottleneck. They also report that N-back accuracy correlates with MMLU Pro, GPQA and IFEval. They draw no conclusions about individual-neuron polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses N-back behavior, representation geometry, attention analyses, and residual-stream interventions; it does not use neuron visualization or the SoLU method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported results vary with memory load and evaluation mode (autoregressive versus teacher forcing); representation measures also vary across layer depth. The optimized intervention gains vary by model strength.

fits_no_version.finding: N-back performance declines with memory load, and retrieval errors are biased toward recent non-target items. Lure, set-size and transition manipulations predict accuracy (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs show human-like working-memory interference in N-back tasks, with recency and content biases that grow with memory load.

fits_no_version.finding: Multiple memory items stay partly entangled in residual-stream representations, especially at higher loads. Letter identity is progressively suppressed and the target aligns with the readout late. Suppressing letter-identity directions improved accuracy in the best searched configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context superposition: during N-back, active contextual items share overlapping activation directions, and this overlap relates to retrieval errors.

record.problems: For the intervention, the best configuration was selected and evaluated on the same trials, so held-out generalization remains untested. Intervention analysis covered a subset of models and used 50 trials per condition. The authors also note that their geometric evidence does not establish a dimensional bottleneck.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted detailed benchmark correlations, attention-head results, and individual baseline accuracy entries because they do not directly bear on neuron polysemanticity or the in-context entanglement findings cataloged here.

untested.parts: Vision-model neurons responding to unrelated images: not studied.
Share of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how it varies by layer: not measured.
Superposition of more sparse features than neurons as the cause of polysemanticity: not tested. Only an analogy is drawn, and no dimensional bottleneck is established.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure: not studied.
Dependence on activation function, architecture or regularization, and the performance cost of reducing polysemanticity: not studied.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons as detecting one shared feature: not studied.
Dependence on activation-range sampling or explanation scoring: not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The superposition terminology could cause this study to be mistaken for evidence on V3. It is not: the representations analysed are averaged residual-stream states, not neurons, and no feature-capacity analysis is done. The text says five models were in the intervention, but Figure 5 lists six model labels. The attention analysis uses Llama3.2-3B, which is not among the 10 evaluated models. The system-prompt text in the paper is task material for the evaluated models, not instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron responses to unrelated image inputs in vision models.
Whether MLP neurons in language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how common this is across layers.
Whether neurons are polysemantic because more sparse features than neurons are packed together; the study does not measure neuron-level features or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Changes in neuron polysemanticity due to activation, architecture, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing it.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether neuron polysemanticity depends on activation-range sampling or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: 10 instruction-tuned LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured N-back performance across memory loads under autoregressive evaluation.
rows.baseline: κ = 0 denotes chance level; κ = 1 denotes perfect performance.
rows.value: Performance declined as memory load increased; most models approached chance by 3- or 4-back.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for model results in text
rows.note: Reported as a qualitative result across the tested LLMs; this measures working-memory limits, not neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Behavioural N-back accuracy (Cohen's κ). It is not a neuron-level measure, and the state against the claim cannot be determined. Table 4 also gives per-model accuracies that the row does not cite.

rows.subject: 10 instruction-tuned LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured probability assigned to target and recent non-target memory items.
rows.measure: Temporal retrieval-probability kernel across relative offsets
rows.value: Retrieval assigned disproportionate probability mass to recent non-target items, and this recency bias grew with memory load.
rows.note: The paper describes this as evidence that competing memories influence retrieval.
rows.check: Behavioural recency kernel (retrieval weight on recent non-target items); unrelated to neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: LLMs (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment of current-item representations with letter-identity representations across layers.

conditions.value: five sampled transformer depths, summarized by layer quantile

rows.measure: Cosine alignment between current-item and letter-identity representations
rows.note: This is a representation-level measure of letter identity during the N-back task, not a measurement of individual neuron meanings.
rows.check: Residual-stream representation alignment with letter-identity representations, not individual neurons; the claim's effect is not measurable from it.

rows.subject: LLMs (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Measured similarity among representations grouped by relative stimulus position across layers.

conditions.value: five sampled transformer depths, summarized by layer quantile

rows.measure: Mean absolute off-diagonal similarity among relative-position representations
rows.value: Representations became more separated through middle layers and partially re-converged in late layers; higher loads retained greater overlap.
rows.note: The authors characterize the remaining overlap as partial entanglement among active memory representations.
rows.check: Overlap among relative-position representations, which the authors call 'in-context superposition'. This is entanglement of contextual items in activation space, not polysemantic neurons. The authors say it does not establish a dimensional bottleneck.

rows.subject: LLMs (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment of target representations with corresponding output readout directions across layers.

conditions.value: five sampled transformer depths, summarized by layer quantile

rows.measure: Cosine alignment of centered target representations with readout directions
rows.value: Alignment remained low in early and middle layers and rose sharply near the end of processing.
rows.note: This is a task-specific representation/readout result, not a neuron-level semantic explanation.
rows.check: Readout alignment is a task-specific geometry measure, not a neuron-level one.

rows.subject: Five LLMs in the intervention subset (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Searched interventions that suppressed selected letter-identity directions in the residual stream at answer positions.

conditions.value: best configuration over directions, strengths, and two early sampled depths; 50 trials per condition

rows.baseline: Matched-seed baseline accuracy; numerical values not stated in text.
rows.value: The best configurations in the search produced aggregate N-back gains; gains were larger in weaker models.
rows.note: Configurations were selected and evaluated on the same trials; the paper says generalization to held-out trials remains untested. Negative gains were clamped to zero in the plotted summary.
rows.check: Best-in-sweep intervention gains, selected and evaluated on the same trials; it is closer to the study's own method result than to a measurement of the claim. Subject: Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-2B, Llama3-8B, Gemma3-4B, Gemma3-1B per Figure 5. That is six model labels, although the text says five LLMs.
